## A Language Fading Away: The Death of the Last Bell Ringers

In Almuñécar, the international recognition of manual bell ringing as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO coexists with a paradox that is hard to ignore: generational transmission has completely broken down. While international bodies safeguard the symbolic value of this practice, in the towers of this town in Granada, the knowledge is concentrated in just three men over the age of seventy. None of them has an apprentice waiting for their turn by the rope.

The contrast with other Spanish regions is devastating. In León, bell ringers preserve a tradition documented for centuries, passed down from parents to children and maintained through gatherings such as the one in Villavante, which has been held for nearly four decades. There, the craft is learned from childhood, when children accompany their elders to the tower and memorize the rhythms by listening, repeating, and making mistakes. In Almuñécar, that thread has been cut without anyone knowing how to tie it back together.

The local brotherhoods, historically responsible for managing the bell ringing, acknowledge the gravity of the problem. Without urgency, without a structured training program, the knowledge accumulated over centuries will be lost in less than a decade. This is not a catastrophist hypothesis: one only needs to do the math. If the three active bell ringers are all over seventy, biology imposes a timeline that no heritage declaration can stop.

Manual bell ringing is neither a folkloric adornment nor a relic for tourists. It is a complete language, with its own grammar, syntax, and local dialects. Every peal, every pause, every acceleration communicates something different: a wedding does not sound the same as a funeral, a fire warning is not confused with the call to mass. Whoever masters this code possesses a communicative competence that no mobile application has managed to replicate with the same emotional depth.

In Almuñécar, the three bell ringers who still climb the towers bear a knowledge that no longer interests the younger generations. The reasons are multiple and intertwined: the mechanization of the bell towers, the depopulation of historic centers, the loss of centrality of parish life. But the result is the same: no one asks, no one observes, no one asks to learn. The craft is fading away in silence, precisely in the place where silence was never an option.

UNESCO declared manual bell ringing an Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2022, following a candidacy promoted by several European countries. The recognition was accompanied by solemn speeches and safeguarding commitments. However, in Almuñécar, as in so many other municipalities in the southern peninsula, the declaration has not altered the daily reality of the towers. The bell ringers continue to climb the spiral staircases with the same worn-out knees and the same uncertainty about who will take their place.

The comparison with León is especially painful because it demonstrates that continuity is possible when there is a collective will to maintain it. There, bell ringers are not an ethnographic rarity: they are respected figures, integrated into community life, with a status that attracts young people. In Almuñécar, the craft has been reduced to a practice for the elderly, a custom that is tolerated as long as it doesn't bother anyone too much and that will disappear without anyone raising their voice.

The local brotherhoods acknowledge that there is no emergency plan. There are no bell ringing schools, no introductory workshops, no recruitment campaigns among teenagers. Nor is there a systematic record of the area's traditional bell tolls, those local nuances that distinguish the ringing of Almuñécar from that of any other Andalusian town. When the three current bell ringers stop climbing the towers, they will take with them a sonic vocabulary that no recording will be able to fully reconstruct.

The problem is not exclusive to Almuñécar. In most municipalities along the coast of Granada, the mechanization of bell towers advanced over the past decades with the promise of efficiency and savings. Electric motors replaced hands, digital programmers replaced human memory. What was gained in punctuality was lost in nuance: a motor can reproduce a pre-recorded toll, but it cannot improvise, it cannot adapt the rhythm to the emotion of the moment, it cannot engage in a dialogue with the community.

The three bell ringers of Almuñécar represent the last generation of a lineage documented since the mid-16th century in the town's chapter acts. Their hands hold the memory of thousands of tolls: patron saint festivals, funerals, storm alerts, council calls. That memory is not written in any manual, it cannot be downloaded from the internet, it is not learned in an intensive course. It is transmitted through contact, through repetition, through years of living alongside the sound and the tower.

Time is running out. Every year that passes without a replacement emerging is a year of knowledge eroding, a year of nuances fading away. The brotherhoods know it, the bell ringers know it, the institutions know it. But knowing is not enough. An active commitment is needed, a collective decision that this language does not deserve to die in silence. And that decision, for now, has not been made in Almuñécar.

The UNESCO declaration should have been a turning point, a spur to act before it was too late. Instead, it has become an uncomfortable reminder of the distance separating official discourse from local reality. While in Pamplona academic conferences are held on the value of manual bell ringing, in Almuñécar the three bell ringers climb the towers without knowing if they will be the last to do so.

The language of the bells is slowly fading, like an echo receding into the mountains. Every manual toll that still rings out in Almuñécar is an act of resistance, an affirmation that this code remains alive as long as there are hands to play it. But resistance has an expiration date. And that date is approaching faster than the brotherhoods are willing to admit in public.
